title: Holiday Decoration Storage Hacks: How to Pack Ornaments, Lights and Garland
seoTitle: Holiday Decoration Storage Hacks That Save Setup Time
excerpt: Holiday decoration storage hacks for ornaments, string lights, garland and small parts: how to sort by job, which containers to use, where to store the bins and a January pack-up routine.
imageCaption: Clear lidded storage bins stacked on a basement shelf, holding glass ornaments in divided inserts, coiled string lights and folded garland. AI-generated illustration of a general idea.
content: The best **holiday decoration storage hacks** are simple: sort decorations by job before they go into storage, give fragile ornaments divided boxes, wind every light strand flat around a piece of cardboard, use clear lidded bins you can read from the outside, and keep a small "first out" bin with hooks, cords and tape on top of the stack. Store everything in a cool, dry spot you can reach without moving the whole garage.

When you bring the decoration bins down, use the opportunity to fix the storage system: you can see exactly what broke, tangled or went missing last year. This guide covers how to sort decorations, the storage hacks that protect ornaments and lights, where to keep the bins, and a simple routine for packing everything away in January so next year's setup involves less searching and untangling.
## Holiday Decoration Storage Hacks at a Glance

Use this table to match each type of decoration with the container and the hack that keeps it safe. Four to six bins is a starting layout for the categories in this guide, not a measured household average or a limit. Adjust the number to the size and fragility of your own collection.

| Decoration | Best container | Storage hack | Common mistake |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Glass and fragile ornaments | Divided box with a lid | One ornament per compartment, heavy ones at the bottom | Loose ornaments wrapped in tissue in a deep tote |
| String lights | Flat cardboard wrap inside a bin | Test, wind flat, tape the plug end | Balling lights up in a bag |
| Garland and wreaths | Wide fabric bin or wreath bag | Coil loosely, store on top so nothing crushes it | Stuffing it into a small box |
| Stockings, tree skirts, linens | Fabric bin or vacuum bag | Wash or air out first, then fold loosely | Storing them damp |
| Small parts (hooks, clips, timers) | Small clear snap boxes | One box per item type, packed in the first-out bin | Loose in the bottom of a tote |
| Tabletop and village pieces | Original box or padded bin | Photograph the layout before packing | Mixing them with ornaments |
## Sort Decorations by Job, Not by Room

Most decoration chaos comes from packing whatever is closest into whichever bin is open. A better rule is to group items by how they need to be handled. Fragile items need padding, lights need untangling protection, soft items need dryness, and small parts need to be findable.

![Diagram of four decoration storage groups: fragile ornaments in divided boxes, lights and cords wound flat and tested, soft decor such as garland and stockings in a fabric bin, and a first-out bin with hooks, extension cords, timers and tape. Diagram: Sesoris](/images/blog/holiday-decoration-storage-hacks-zones.webp)

1. **Fragile.** Glass ornaments, ceramic pieces and anything that chips.
2. **Lights and cords.** Every string of lights, extension cords, timers and remotes.
3. **Soft decor.** Garland, stockings, tree skirts, pillow covers and table runners.
4. **First out.** The handful of things you need on setup day before anything else: ornament hooks, cord clips, a timer, tape, scissors and a spare bulb kit.

Before you sort, set aside anything broken, faded or unused for two seasons. Our guide to [decluttering home decor](/blog/decluttering-home-decor) has a simple keep, donate or toss method that works well for decorations, and the [declutter your house](/blog/declutter-your-house) checklist helps if the bins are only one part of a bigger cleanup.
## Hack 1: Give Every Ornament Its Own Compartment

Fragile ornaments can chip when they knock against each other. A divided box with a lid keeps pieces separated, but compartments do not replace cushioning. Wrap delicate pieces individually in suitable clean, dry padding, put one ornament in each compartment and keep heavier pieces in a separate bottom box so they cannot press onto lighter ones.

You do not need a box sold specifically for ornaments. A fabric storage box with movable dividers and a clear zip-top lid, such as our [16-compartment storage box](/product/under-bed-shoe-storage-box-16-compartments) (17 x 17 x 12.4 inches), works the same way. Adjust the dividers so each slot fits snugly, and the clear lid lets you see which ornaments are inside without opening it.

![A gray fabric storage box with 16 compartments formed by movable dividers and a clear zippered lid, shown filled with pairs of flats. Photo: Sesoris product catalog](/images/blog/holiday-decoration-storage-hacks-compartment-box.webp)

For very small or delicate pieces, egg cartons and small cups also work as dividers inside a larger bin. Whatever you use, write the contents on a tag on two sides of the box so you can read it from any angle on a shelf.
## Hack 2: Wind Lights Flat Around Cardboard

Inspect each light strand while it is unplugged before you test it. Check the cord, sockets and connections, and discard damaged sets rather than connecting them to power. The [CPSC holiday decoration safety guide](https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/611.pdf) identifies broken sockets, frayed or bare wires and loose connections as warning signs. Only test an undamaged strand, then unplug it before changing a bulb, winding it around cardboard or putting it away. Follow the light manufacturer's instructions for replacement bulbs and storage.

Then cut a rectangle of sturdy cardboard about the size of a sheet of paper, notch one short edge, slide the plug end into the notch and wind the strand around the board in flat, even loops. Tape the other end down and write the length or the room it belongs to on the board.

![A strand of unlit holiday string lights wound neatly around a flat piece of notched cardboard on a wooden table, next to a coiled extension cord with a hook-and-loop strap and a small clear bin. AI-generated illustration of a general idea](/images/blog/holiday-decoration-storage-hacks-lights.webp)

- Wind outdoor and indoor lights on separate boards so you never hang an indoor strand outside.
- Coil extension cords loosely and secure them with a hook-and-loop strap rather than knotting them.
- Keep timers and remotes in a small labeled box in the first-out bin, not loose in the lights bin.
- Store light boards standing on their edge so the strands are not crushed under heavy items.
## Hack 3: Use Small Clear Boxes for Tiny Parts

Ornament hooks, spare bulbs, fuses, cord clips and the tiny pieces of a tabletop village are the first things to disappear. Small clear snap boxes keep each type separate and visible. Our [clear plastic storage boxes](/product/clear-plastic-storage-boxes-24-pack) come in two sizes, 5.11 x 3.14 x 1.18 inches and 2.16 x 2.16 x 0.78 inches, with hinged snap lids that stay closed if the box is turned over in a bin.

![Small clear plastic boxes with hinged snap lids in two sizes, filled with paper clips, beads and small jewelry, shown on a white background. Photo: Sesoris product catalog](/images/blog/holiday-decoration-storage-hacks-small-boxes.webp)
Put all the small boxes together in the first-out bin. On setup day, that one bin gives you hooks for the tree, clips for the gutters and fresh bulbs for any strand that flickers.
## Hack 4: Clear Bins, Matching Lids and Visible Labels

Opaque totes in different sizes are hard to stack and harder to search. Switch gradually to clear bins with matching lids in one or two sizes. You can see what is inside, the stack stays stable, and a label on the short end tells you the contents when the bin sits on a shelf.

Label by group and by room, for example "Fragile, tree ornaments" or "Lights, porch". Number the bins and keep a short list on your phone of what is in each number. When someone asks where the stockings are, you check the list instead of opening six boxes.
## Where to Store Holiday Decorations
The right spot depends on your home, but the best places share three traits: they stay dry, they do not swing between very hot and very cold, and you can reach them without moving everything else.

Before closing a bin, check fabric folds, the underside of wreaths and the bin itself for dampness. The [EPA guide to mold and moisture in the home](https://www.epa.gov/mold/brief-guide-mold-moisture-and-your-home) explains that moisture control is the key to mold prevention and recommends drying items completely. Let decorations dry fully before packing; a closed lid is not a substitute for drying or for fixing a damp storage location. Follow the care label when cleaning a delicate or sentimental piece.

| Location | Works well for | Watch out for | Tip |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Basement shelving | Most bins, especially heavy ones | Dampness near the floor | Keep bins on shelves, not directly on concrete |
| Garage shelves | Outdoor decor, lights, sturdy plastic items | Heat and cold swings | Avoid storing candles or delicate glass here |
| Closet shelf or under-stairs closet | Fragile ornaments and soft decor | Limited height | Use the top shelf for light bins |
| Under the bed | Flat items, wrapping supplies, tree skirts | Dust | Choose bins with zip or snap lids |
| Attic | Lightweight, non-fragile items | Temperature extremes | Leave delicate and heat-sensitive items elsewhere |

If your bins currently live on the garage floor, our guides to [basement storage ideas](/blog/basement-storage-ideas), [best garage storage solutions](/blog/best-garage-storage-solutions) and [under-stairs closet storage](/blog/under-stairs-closet-storage-ideas) show shelving setups that free up space. For flat items, the [under-bed storage containers](/blog/best-under-bed-storage-containers-review-buying-guide-2026) review compares lid styles and sizes.
## Hack 5: Pack a First-Out Bin and a Last-In Bin

Two special bins make the whole season smoother. The **first-out bin** holds everything you need before anything else on setup day: hooks, extension cords, timers, tape, scissors, spare bulbs and a small tool kit. Put it on top of the stack or at the front of the shelf.

The **last-in bin** is empty when you take decorations out. Use it to store the everyday decor you swap out for the season, such as throw pillows, a regular wreath or table centerpieces. When the holidays end, the decorations go back into their bins and your everyday items come out of this one, so nothing ends up homeless on a counter for weeks.
## A Simple Routine for Packing Up in January
Most of the work of next year's setup happens when you pack up. Give yourself one afternoon and follow the same order every year.

1. **Take photos** of the tree, mantel and tabletop displays before you take anything down.
2. **Inspect unplugged lights** and discard damaged sets. Test only undamaged strands, then unplug them again before packing.
3. **Gather by group** on a clear table: fragile, lights, soft and small parts.
4. **Clean and dry** stockings, linens and tree skirts before folding them.
5. **Pack by group**, keeping heavy items separate from fragile pieces.
6. **Label and number** each bin, and update the list on your phone.
7. **Return everyday decor** from the last-in bin and store the empty bins nested together.

This routine pairs well with the seasonal tasks in our [winter home maintenance checklist](/blog/winter-home-maintenance-checklist), and if you bake for the holidays, our [holiday cookie storage containers](/blog/holiday-cookie-storage-containers) and [kitchen wrap organizer ideas](/blog/kitchen-wrap-organizer-ideas) guides cover the kitchen side of the season. For decorating ideas once everything is unpacked, see [holiday home decor ideas](/blog/holiday-home-decor-ideas).
## Common Holiday Storage Mistakes

- **Storing decorations damp.** Garland, wreaths and fabric items that go into a bin damp can grow mildew by next year.
- **Overfilling bins.** A bin that needs to be forced shut crushes what is inside and cracks the lid.
- **Mixing fragile and heavy items.** A ceramic piece on top of glass ornaments is how breakage happens.
- **Keeping everything.** Broken, faded and unused items take up shelf space that could hold what you love.
- **Hiding the first-out bin.** If the hooks and cords are at the bottom of the stack, setup starts with unpacking everything.
## Frequently Asked Questions
**Q: What is the best way to store Christmas ornaments?**

Wrap delicate ornaments in suitable clean, dry padding and place one in each compartment of a lidded box. Keep heavier pieces in a separate bottom box, rather than letting them press on fragile ones. Divided boxes, egg cartons or movable dividers can help separate pieces. Label the box on two sides and keep it on a shelf where nothing heavy sits on top.
**Q: How do I keep Christmas lights from tangling?**

Inspect each unplugged strand first and discard damaged sets. Test only an undamaged strand, unplug it again, then wind it flat around a notched piece of cardboard, starting with the plug end tucked into the notch. Tape the far end down and label the board. Store the boards on their edge inside a bin so they are not crushed.
**Q: Is it okay to store holiday decorations in the garage?**

Sturdy items such as plastic outdoor decor and light boards usually handle a garage well if they sit on shelves in sealed bins. Avoid storing candles, delicate glass and anything heat-sensitive there, because many garages get very hot in summer and cold in winter.
**Q: Are clear bins better than opaque totes for decorations?**

For most homes, yes. Clear bins let you see the contents without opening them, which saves time on setup day. Opaque bins are useful only for items that fade in light, such as some fabrics, and only if they are clearly labeled.
**Q: How many storage bins do I need for holiday decorations?**

Use four to six as a starting layout, not a household average: one or two for fragile ornaments, one for lights and cords, one for soft decor, one first-out bin and one last-in bin for everyday decor. Your collection may need fewer or more. Start with what you own and add bins only when a group clearly needs more room.
**Q: How should I store artificial wreaths and garland?**

Coil garland loosely and store it in a wide fabric bin or bag on top of the stack so nothing presses on it. Hang wreaths on a hook in a closet or keep them in a round wreath bag. Make sure both are completely dry before you pack them away.
**Q: When should I organize my holiday decoration storage?**

The easiest time is when you pack up in January, because you can see what broke and what you did not use. A quick check in mid-November, when the bins come down, lets you replace damaged lights and missing hooks before decorating starts.
**Q: What should go in a first-out bin?**

Everything you need before decorating starts: ornament hooks, extension cords, outlet timers, tape, scissors, cord clips, spare bulbs and fuses, and a small tool kit. Keep it on top of the stack so it is the first thing you open.
## Final Thoughts

Good holiday decoration storage is less about buying special containers and more about a few habits: sort by job, protect each ornament and light strand, label clear bins on the outside and keep a first-out bin on top. Spend one afternoon setting this up when you pack away this season, and next November your decorations will come out in order, ready to hang.
